rationale:
This is today's slate for 2026-11-06: 1 long video, 3 Shorts and 1 carousel. Every piece stays in the GLP-1 focus and follows the 11-03 growth playbook.

**Long video.** L1 is the next item on the playbook's Lane A ship list, "Why Am I So Tired on Tirzepatide?" Stopping and birth control already shipped on 11-04 and 11-05. The Hair Loss redo needs a fix and re-upload of the existing video, which is the publisher's job, so it isn't a new script. Fatigue is evergreen and well documented: the label rates (5–7% vs 3% on placebo), NHS tiredness pages and the joint nutrition advisory. Shorter November days give the intro a hook, and the body rests on settled evidence. No live Lane A video answers it yet. It sits next to Side Effects and What to Eat, so it follows the Bones & Muscle model for suggested-video pickup. The 10-31 fatigue Short becomes a feeder.

**Shorts.**
- **S1 (08:00):** a calm "Will it…?" body-worry Short about Thanksgiving dinner. It's the top rising radar topic (momentum 87, search peak Nov 18–27). It feeds the slow Thanksgiving long video and isn't a hair topic.
- **S2 (13:00):** a fresh randomized result with tirzepatide named first: TOGETHER-PsA, being presented at ACR this week. The radar marked it caution, so the angle is evidence-first, with figures checked against Lilly's primary release.
- **S3 (20:00):** the spin-off of L1 and the funnel Short. It asks a new question, whether low blood sugar is behind tiredness. That's a myth correction: in the trials, low blood sugar was uncommon unless someone also used insulin or a sulfonylurea.

**Skipped.**
- SURMOUNT-5 head-to-head: two Shorts in the last 30 days (10-15, 10-17).
- Prediabetes: covered 11-04.
- Retatrutide knee: done 11-02, and the plenary data aren't out until 11-08.
- Injection site: Short on 11-02, and the long video comes later in the order.
- Hair Shorts: banned this week.
- Pill and earnings angles: business framing.

**Carousel.** Carousels reach almost nobody, so per the playbook C1 reuses only the verified 11-04 sick-day and dehydration Short text. It's seasonal and matches L1's fluids theme.

**Mix.**
- Emerging or rising: S1, S2.
- Evergreen with a timely hook: L1, C1.
- Myth correction: S3.

**Pillars:** get-the-most ×2, life-on-glp1, beyond-weight, myths. No more than 2 per pillar.

**Body systems:** energy, stomach, joints, blood sugar, fluids and kidneys. No three pieces on the same one.

pieces.topic: Fatigue on tirzepatide: how often it was reported (Zepbound label: 5%, 6% and 7% by dose vs 3% on placebo, pooled SURMOUNT-1 and -2), likely everyday contributors (eating much less, low fluids, too little protein, poor sleep, GI side effects), and when tiredness is a reason to call the prescriber
pieces.angle:
Lane A (log 'lane: A'; publisher adds it to the 'Life on Tirzepatide' playlist). Runs 8–12 min at 14:00 ET.

The first spoken sentence answers the title: 'Tiredness is a listed side effect of tirzepatide, but it was uncommon in the trials: about 5 to 7 in 100 people across doses, versus 3 in 100 on placebo.' Then a 'you' scenario: it's November, the days are shorter, you're eating far less, and you're dragging by 3 pm. One seasonal line in the intro at most. The body rests on the label, the NHS tiredness pages (2023) and the 2025 ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS advisory.

Chapters, named as searched questions:
(1) Is fatigue a side effect of tirzepatide? Give the label's per-dose rates vs placebo exactly as printed, with the pooled-trial population. Write the narration numbers as words and check every one in speech-to-text.
(2) Why might you feel tired? Possible contributors, each worded 'can' and never as proven cause: eating much less, low fluids, skipped protein, poor sleep, and nausea or diarrhoea. The general causes come from NHS, tagged NHS.
(3) Could it be dehydration? Use the label's dehydration and kidney wording exactly. Sipping fluids, unless you've been told to limit them, is our own tip with no tag.
(4) Does protein help energy? Credit only what the advisory says (getting enough protein). The kidney caveat goes in.
(5) What about sleep and movement? General guidance only. Strength training follows the advisory's exact wording, started gently.
(6) Could something else be going on? Questions for your clinician, including whether blood tests (e.g. iron, thyroid) make sense. No supplement promises.
(7) When should you call your prescriber? Dizziness or fainting, vomiting or diarrhoea with signs of dehydration, and, for people who also use insulin or a sulfonylurea, low blood sugar signs, all in label wording.

Format and safety rules:
- Re-hook every 45–75 s.
- One subscribe ask, after the chapter 2–4 'what helps' payoff.
- No dosing or titration content. Never say 'adjust your dose'.
- Include 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own', one GI line, 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. Each must be both spoken and in the on-screen field.
- Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' No spoken titles. The publisher links Side Effects or What to Eat.
- Thumbnail: a state change from drained to recharged, 4 words or fewer, not reusing title words (e.g. 'Running on Empty?' → answered). One labelled character, calm mood, no body imagery.

pieces.why: It's the next Lane A topic on this week's ship list (radar momentum 82, a seasonal bump as winter starts), and no live long video answers it. It's built on label and NHS evidence that holds up to fact-checking, and it sits next to Side Effects for suggested-video pickup.

pieces.topic: Thanksgiving dinner on tirzepatide: why you may feel full fast at a big meal (slower gastric emptying, label wording) and calm ways to make the day easier
pieces.angle:
08:00 body-worry Short, 60–85 s, 170 words or fewer.

Answer within 10 s: 'Will Thanksgiving dinner make you sick on tirzepatide? Not necessarily, but a big, rich meal may sit heavier, because tirzepatide can slow how fast food leaves your stomach' (label wording).

The new fact is the label's gastric-emptying wording plus the common GI side effects it lists. Then our own untagged tips:
- start with a small plate built around turkey or another protein you enjoy
- eat slowly
- stop at comfortably full
- sip fluids unless you've been told to limit them

Alcohol: make no sourced claim; just say ask your prescriber. People who also use insulin or a sulfonylurea should ask their prescriber about the holiday meal (label: higher low-blood-sugar risk).

Red flag, in label wording: severe stomach pain that won't go away means contact your healthcare provider.

Also required:
- 'Don't skip, move or change your injection or dose around the holiday on your own.'
- No guilt, no foods labelled 'bad', no calorie talk.
- Exp F line second to last, then 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, both spoken and on screen.
- Last line: 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.' The publisher puts the Thanksgiving long video's link on description line 1.

Mix at masking 0.02 or lower.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide plus ixekizumab for psoriatic arthritis with obesity: the TOGETHER-PsA randomized Phase 3b trial, presented at ACR Convergence 2026 (6–11 Nov)
pieces.angle: Evergreen framing: 'Tirzepatide and Psoriatic Arthritis: What a Trial Found' (don't call it new). Open: 'In a randomized trial in adults with active psoriatic arthritis and overweight or obesity, adding tirzepatide to the arthritis drug ixekizumab was compared with ixekizumab alone.' Credit: 'TOGETHER-PsA, Arthritis & Rheumatology, 2026; open-label, company-funded'. No ACR Convergence attribution. Give 138 vs 133 people, week 36, the composite (ACR50 plus at least 10% weight loss) 31.7% vs 0.8%, and ACR50 alone 33.5% vs 20.4%. Week-52 figures go in only if confirmed from a primary Lilly release or abstract, labelled as conference/company-reported. Keep: one trial; tirzepatide isn't approved to treat psoriatic arthritis; weight is one measure among joint outcomes; the qualitative GI line; 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own; talk to your rheumatologist or prescriber'; the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line; loop to the opening.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide and Psoriatic Arthritis: What a Trial Found
pieces.why: It's a fresh randomized, tirzepatide-named result presented at ACR this week, with very little creator coverage. It fills the playbook's 13:00 fresh-randomized-result slot and the 'benefits beyond weight' pillar. | fact-check: The trial is real, but the brief gets its status wrong. TOGETHER-PsA is a Phase 3b, randomized, OPEN-LABEL, 52-week trial. Topline results came out in January 2026. It was presented as a late-breaker at AAD in March 2026 and is already PEER-REVIEWED in Arthritis & Rheumatology 2026 (doi:10.1002/art.70134). Week-52 data were reported in September 2026. So 'presented at ACR Convergence 2026', 'fresh randomized result' and 'company-reported, not yet peer-reviewed' are all inaccurate. The craft notes also bar calling it 'new' because the data are more than 3 months old. It doesn't meet the 13:00 'fresh randomized result' criterion. The scheduler should know this, and could run it as an evergreen Short or move it to a slot where freshness isn't required. Confirmed facts: 271 adults with active PsA and BMI ≥30, or BMI 27–29.9 plus at least one weight-related condition (so say 'overweight or obesity', not 'obesity'). Arms: ixekizumab + tirzepatide n=138 vs ixekizumab alone n=133. Primary composite at week 36: ACR50 (at least a 50% improvement in arthritis signs and symptoms) AND ≥10% weight reduction, 31.7% vs 0.8%. ACR50 alone at week 36: 33.5% vs 20.4%. Weight is half of the composite, so the 31.7% vs 0.8% gap mostly reflects the weight half. Pair it with the ACR50-alone figure so the joint benefit isn't overstated. Per-arm GI rates weren't found in the secondary sources. Use a qualitative GI line ('stomach side effects such as nausea were more common with tirzepatide') unless the paper's per-arm figures are opened and confirmed. Sources checked: https://www.healio.com/news/rheumatology/20260609/taltz-plus-tirzepatide-superior-to-monotherapy-in-psoriatic-arthritis-alongside-obesity ; https://www.dermatologytimes.com/view/eli-lilly-trial-shows-superior-outcomes-with-ixekizumab-and-tirzepatide-in-patients-with-psa-and-obesity ; https://www.hcplive.com/view/xekizumab-tirzepatide-sustains-1-year-gains-psoriatic-disease-obesity

pieces.topic: Is low blood sugar why you feel tired on tirzepatide? How uncommon hypoglycemia was in SURMOUNT-1 (people without diabetes) vs the label's higher risk when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea
pieces.angle:
20:00 funnel Short (Exp D) and spin-off of L1. It asks one fresh question, about low blood sugar, rather than re-cutting L1 or repeating the 10-31 fatigue Short. 60–85 s, 170 words or fewer.

Answer within 10 s: 'Tired or shaky on tirzepatide? Low blood sugar is a common worry, but in the big obesity trial in people without diabetes it was uncommon.' Copy the per-arm hypoglycemia rates vs placebo exactly from NEJM 2022 SURMOUNT-1 or the label, with the population named. If they can't be confirmed, use the label's qualitative wording instead.

The new fact is the label's warning that the risk of low blood sugar is higher when tirzepatide is used with insulin or a sulfonylurea, so ask your prescriber. Give the low blood sugar signs in label wording. One line: other everyday causes of tiredness are covered in the full video.

Also required:
- 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.'
- One GI line.
- 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, both spoken and on screen.
- No Exp F line, no spoken titles.
- Last line: 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.'

L1's URL goes on description line 1 only once it's verified live. Otherwise link Side Effects and don't count this Short toward Exp D. Mix at 0.02 or lower.

pieces.topic: Sick on tirzepatide this cold and flu season: why vomiting or diarrhoea can lead to dehydration, the label's kidney warning, and when to call your prescriber (reused from the verified 11-04 Short)
pieces.angle: Same 7 slides, reusing only verified 11-04 text. Slide 2 in label wording: 'The tirzepatide label notes reports of kidney problems, including sudden kidney injury, mostly in people who lost fluids through nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea.' Drop 'rare' unless the verified script sourced it. Slide 6 keeps 'contact your prescriber or healthcare provider right away' and 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own; ask your prescriber what to do on sick days.' Slide 7: 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Sick on Tirzepatide? Fluids, Kidneys and When to Call
pieces.why: The scheduler asked for a carousel, and the playbook says to reuse verified Short text only. Flu season is starting (radar momentum 80), and the fluids theme matches today's fatigue long video. | fact-check: Run it only if the scheduler explicitly asked for it. Carousels reach 0–4 people and are stopped by default. Run it only if the 11-04 sick-day Short is confirmed verified and published; otherwise drop it. Slide 2's wording is a problem. The Zepbound/Mounjaro label (section 5, acute kidney injury due to volume depletion) says there have been postmarketing reports of acute kidney injury and worsening chronic renal failure, sometimes needing hemodialysis, and that most of these occurred in patients who had nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea leading to volume depletion (dehydration). The label doesn't use the word 'rare'. Use 'rare' only if the verified 11-04 script printed it with a source that says it. 'Mostly' must stay attached to 'reported events', not to people generally. Slide 4's 'ask a pharmacist before cold or flu remedies' stays untagged, as our own tip. Slide 5's sick-day plan: say 'ask your prescriber', with no instructions about dose changes. No emoji, and no skip-a-dose content.
